claim: Inhibiting actomyosin contraction blocked oscillations in the epithelium after shear.
source: Inhibiting actomyosin contraction or E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion blocked oscillations, whereas stabilizing actin filaments prolonged oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using blebbistatin to inhibit myosin II, which blocked oscillatory cell movements.

claim: Inhibiting E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion blocked oscillations in the epithelium after shear.
source: Inhibiting actomyosin contraction or E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion blocked oscillations, whereas stabilizing actin filaments prolonged oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using T151 cells expressing truncated E-cadherin, which did not exhibit oscillatory movements.

claim: Stabilizing actin filaments prolonged oscillations in the epithelium after shear.
source: Inhibiting actomyosin contraction or E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion blocked oscillations, whereas stabilizing actin filaments prolonged oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using jasplakinolide to stabilize actin filaments, which resulted in prolonged oscillations.

claim: A shear-induced mechanical event at the shear plane is relayed across the epithelium by actomyosin contraction linked through E-cadherin.
source: Combining these data with a model of epithelium mechanics supports a mechanism involving the generation of a shear-induced mechanical event at the shear plane which is then relayed across the epithelium by actomyosin contraction linked through E-cadherin.
evidence: This claim is supported by combining experimental data with mechanical modeling that includes stiffness, damping, and inerter elements.

claim: Shear causes an imbalance of forces in the epithelium, which is gradually dissipated through oscillatory cell movements and actin filament turnover to restore the force balance across the epithelium.
source: This causes an imbalance of forces in the epithelium, which is gradually dissipated through oscillatory cell movements and actin filament turnover to restore the force balance across the epithelium.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of damped oscillations and modeling results showing force dissipation over time.

claim: Mechanical forces play important roles at the single-cell and multicellular levels in tissue biology.
source: Mechanical forces play important roles at the single-cell and multicellular levels in tissue biology (Farge, 2011; Hoffman et al., 2011), including in the regulation of cell shape and movement (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2012; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013; Clément et al., 2017), cell-cycle progression (Campinho et al., 2013; Streichan et al., 2014), cell-division orientation (di Pietro et al., 2016; Gloerich et al., 2017), and gene expression (Aragona et al., 2013; Benham-Pyle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research in the field.

claim: Mechanical forces regulate cell shape and movement.
source: Mechanical forces play important roles at the single-cell and multicellular levels in tissue biology (Farge, 2011; Hoffman et al., 2011), including in the regulation of cell shape and movement (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2012; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013; Clément et al., 2017), cell-cycle progression (Campinho et al., 2013; Streichan et al., 2014), cell-division orientation (di Pietro et al., 2016; Gloerich et al., 2017), and gene expression (Aragona et al., 2013; Benham-Pyle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mechanical forces regulate cell-cycle progression.
source: Mechanical forces play important roles at the single-cell and multicellular levels in tissue biology (Farge, 2011; Hoffman et al., 2011), including in the regulation of cell shape and movement (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2012; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013; Clément et al., 2017), cell-cycle progression (Campinho et al., 2013; Streichan et al., 2014), cell-division orientation (di Pietro et al., 2016; Gloerich et al., 2017), and gene expression (Aragona et al., 2013; Benham-Pyle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mechanical forces regulate cell-division orientation.
source: Mechanical forces play important roles at the single-cell and multicellular levels in tissue biology (Farge, 2011; Hoffman et al., 2011), including in the regulation of cell shape and movement (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2012; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013; Clément et al., 2017), cell-cycle progression (Campinho et al., 2013; Streichan et al., 2014), cell-division orientation (di Pietro et al., 2016; Gloerich et al., 2017), and gene expression (Aragona et al., 2013; Benham-Pyle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mechanical forces regulate gene expression.
source: Mechanical forces play important roles at the single-cell and multicellular levels in tissue biology (Farge, 2011; Hoffman et al., 2011), including in the regulation of cell shape and movement (Aegerter-Wilmsen et al., 2012; Legoff et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2013; Clément et al., 2017), cell-cycle progression (Campinho et al., 2013; Streichan et al., 2014), cell-division orientation (di Pietro et al., 2016; Gloerich et al., 2017), and gene expression (Aragona et al., 2013; Benham-Pyle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous studies have examined mechanical forces by observing the generation of cellular traction forces or by applying external tensile forces to whole cell populations.
source: In general, these effects have been studied by observing the generation of cellular traction forces, or by applying external tensile forces to whole cell populations (Mukundan et al., 2013; Simmons et al., 2011; Tambe et al., 2011; Zaritsky et al., 2015; Micoulet et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research methods.

claim: A few studies have estimated the shear forces between cells from observations of cellular tractions.
source: While a few studies have estimated the shear forces between cells from observations of cellular tractions ( Tambe et al., 2011; Zaritsky et al., 2015), none have perturbed a tissue with direct application of shear loading.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: No prior studies have perturbed a tissue with direct application of shear loading.
source: While a few studies have estimated the shear forces between cells from observations of cellular tractions ( Tambe et al., 2011; Zaritsky et al., 2015), none have perturbed a tissue with direct application of shear loading.
evidence: This claim is supported by a review of prior literature indicating a gap in the field.

claim: In-plane shear forces exist within any solid material under load, such as between groups of cells in tissues under applied or intrinsic forces.
source: In-plane shear forces exist within any solid material under load, such as between groups of cells in tissues under applied or intrinsic forces.
evidence: This claim is based on established principles of mechanics applied to biological tissues.

claim: In-plane shear forces are distinct from shear stresses applied by laminar liquid flow on top of cells that mimic the vasculature.
source: These forces are distinct from shear stresses applied by laminar liquid flow on top of cells that mimic the vasculature.
evidence: This claim distinguishes between two types of shear forces based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tissues spontaneously generate internal shear forces to maintain an external force balance.
source: Tissues spontaneously generate internal shear forces to maintain an external force balance (Prost et al., 2015), and biopolymer networks have been observed to pull inward when sheared on a rheometer (Janmey et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Biopolymer networks have been observed to pull inward when sheared on a rheometer.
source: Tissues spontaneously generate internal shear forces to maintain an external force balance (Prost et al., 2015), and biopolymer networks have been observed to pull inward when sheared on a rheometer (Janmey et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In-plane shear forces are thought to affect the collective behavior of migrating cells in epithelial tissues.
source: In-plane shear forces are thought to affect the collective behavior of migrating cells in epithelial tissues (Tambe et al., 2011; Zaritsky et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ridges that appear in the epithelial tissue forming the pupal Drosophila wing have been attributed to shear forces arising during development.
source: For example, the ridges that appear in the epithelial tissue forming the pupal Drosophila wing have been attributed to shear forces arising during development (Etournay et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Shear forces between migrating cells of the prechordal plate in the zebrafish embryo and cells of the neurectoderm determine the position of the neural anlage.
source: In addition, shear forces between migrating cells of the prechordal plate in the zebrafish embryo and cells of the neurectoderm determine the position of the neural anlage (Smutny et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Local shear forces between groups of cells are important contributors to global effects in tissue motility and organ patterning.
source: These studies suggest that local shear forces between groups of cells are important contributors to global effects in tissue motility and organ patterning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited studies on Drosophila wing and zebrafish embryo development.

claim: How local in-plane shear forces are spread throughout a tissue is not understood.
source: However, how local in-plane shear forces are spread throughout a tissue, which is important for understanding collective tissue behavior, is not understood in part because of the difficulty in applying direct and localized in-plane shear within a tissue.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in current knowledge based on review of the literature.

claim: The difficulty in applying direct and localized in-plane shear within a tissue has limited understanding of how shear forces spread throughout a tissue.
source: However, how local in-plane shear forces are spread throughout a tissue, which is important for understanding collective tissue behavior, is not understood in part because of the difficulty in applying direct and localized in-plane shear within a tissue.
evidence: This claim identifies a technical limitation in the field.

claim: In-plane shear produces local deformations that are propagated into a global migratory response that distributes and dissipates forces through oscillations.
source: We determined that in-plane shear produces local deformations that are propagated into a global migratory response that distributes and dissipates forces through oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the novel shear device and PIV analysis.

claim: Confined epithelia have been shown to oscillate.
source: Confined epithelia, similar to embryos or tumors, have been shown to oscillate (Deforet et al., 2014; Kocgozlu et al., 2016), but the mechanism driving these oscillations is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mechanism driving oscillations in confined epithelia is unknown.
source: Confined epithelia, similar to embryos or tumors, have been shown to oscillate (Deforet et al., 2014; Kocgozlu et al., 2016), but the mechanism driving these oscillations is unknown.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in current knowledge based on review of the literature.

claim: Oscillatory behavior may be important as an intrinsic collective cellular process that follows a shear-induced force imbalance, enabling the probing and maintenance of tension homeostasis within a developing tissue.
source: Such oscillatory behavior may be important as an intrinsic collective cellular process that follows a shear-induced force imbalance, enabling the probing and maintenance of tension homeostasis within a developing tissue.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a potential biological function for the observed oscillations.

claim: The shear device consisted of two parallel 1000 μm x 250 μm suspended planks, one for force actuation and the other for force sensing.
source: The device consisted of two parallel 1000 μm x 250 μm suspended planks, one for force actuation and the other for force sensing.
evidence: This claim describes the design of the experimental device.

claim: Moving the actuation plank applied 100 μm of shear at the midline of a MDCK epithelial cell monolayer.
source: Moving the actuation plank applied 100 μm of shear (resulting in about one radian average cellular shear strain in cells near the mid-plane) at the midline of a Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) epithelial cell monolayer cultured across the surface of both planks (Figure 1A; Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method for applying shear.

claim: 100 μm of shear resulted in about one radian average cellular shear strain in cells near the mid-plane.
source: Moving the actuation plank applied 100 μm of shear (resulting in about one radian average cellular shear strain in cells near the mid-plane) at the midline of a Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) epithelial cell monolayer cultured across the surface of both planks (Figure 1A; Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim provides a calculated measure of cellular strain from the applied shear.

claim: The stiffness of the sensing spring is 0.93 N/m.
source: We calculated force across the monolayer from the displacement of the sensing spring (ks = 0.93 N/m) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Following the application of shear, the epithelium did not rupture or tear.
source: Following the application of shear, the epithelium did not rupture or tear (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), nor was there significant extrusion of dead cells (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual evidence from figures and videos.

claim: Following the application of shear, there was no significant extrusion of dead cells.
source: Following the application of shear, the epithelium did not rupture or tear (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), nor was there significant extrusion of dead cells (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual evidence from videos.

claim: Throughout the response to shear, cells within the epithelium retained their nearest neighbors.
source: Throughout the response, cells within the epithelium retained their nearest neighbors, and new cell adhesions were formed only between daughter cells and their neighbors following division (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual evidence from figures and videos showing cell tracking.

claim: New cell adhesions were formed only between daughter cells and their neighbors following division.
source: Throughout the response, cells within the epithelium retained their nearest neighbors, and new cell adhesions were formed only between daughter cells and their neighbors following division (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual evidence from figures and videos showing cell tracking.

claim: Cells throughout the epithelium began a collective wave of inward y-direction movement toward the shear-plane, which started at the shear-plane and propagated to the opposite edge of the plank within 45 min.
source: Cells throughout the epithelium began a collective wave of inward y-direction movement toward the shear-plane, which started at the shear-plane and propagated to the opposite edge of the plank within 45 min at a rate 10x faster than individual cell velocities (290 vs. 30 μm/h; Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data and kymographs shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The inward movement propagated at a rate 10x faster than individual cell velocities (290 vs. 30 μm/h).
source: Cells throughout the epithelium began a collective wave of inward y-direction movement toward the shear-plane, which started at the shear-plane and propagated to the opposite edge of the plank within 45 min at a rate 10x faster than individual cell velocities (290 vs. 30 μm/h; Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of PIV data.

claim: Inward movement toward the shear-plane was expected because biopolymer networks develop an inward normal stress under applied shear.
source: This inward movement was expected because biopolymer networks develop an inward normal stress under applied shear (Janmey et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on biopolymer networks.

claim: Cells reversed y-direction movements at 7, 11, and 15 hr after shear with decreasing velocity magnitude, behaving as a damped oscillator.
source: In our live epithelium, cells reversed y-direction movements at 7, 11, and 15 hr after shear with decreasing velocity magnitude: they behaved as a damped oscillator (Figure 1D,E), with cells furthest from the shear-plane exhibiting the most movement in the y-direction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data and displacement plots shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Cells furthest from the shear-plane exhibited the most movement in the y-direction.
source: In our live epithelium, cells reversed y-direction movements at 7, 11, and 15 hr after shear with decreasing velocity magnitude: they behaved as a damped oscillator (Figure 1D,E), with cells furthest from the shear-plane exhibiting the most movement in the y-direction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by displacement data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Reversals in y-direction movement propagated from the shear plane outward at 80–100 μm/h.
source: Reversals in y-direction movement propagated from the shear plane outward at 80–100 μm/h.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of PIV data.

claim: Cells adjacent to the shear-plane (2–3 cell layers,<50 μm) were deformed, and moved in the x-direction opposite the applied shear.
source: Cells adjacent to the shear-plane (2–3 cell layers,<50 μm) were deformed, and moved in the x-direction opposite the applied shear (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data and kymographs shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: X-direction movements of cells adjacent to the shear-plane diminished within ~1 hr, and stopped after ~3 hr.
source: These x-direction movements diminished within ~1 hr, and stopped after ~3 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of PIV data over time.

claim: In the deformation zone, y-direction cell movements were small, outward, and short-lived.
source: In this deformation zone, y-direction cell movements were small, outward, and short-lived.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of PIV data in the deformation zone.

claim: Cell oscillations in the y-direction, but not the x-direction, occurred spontaneously without shear.
source: Cell oscillations in the y-direction, but not the x-direction, also occurred spontaneously without shear (Figure 1H–K; Video 3), at a cell velocity 3-4x slower than in the presence of applied shear (9 vs. 30 μm/h).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data from control experiments without shear shown in Figure 1H–K.

claim: Spontaneous oscillations without shear occurred at a cell velocity 3-4x slower than in the presence of applied shear (9 vs. 30 μm/h).
source: Cell oscillations in the y-direction, but not the x-direction, also occurred spontaneously without shear (Figure 1H–K; Video 3), at a cell velocity 3-4x slower than in the presence of applied shear (9 vs. 30 μm/h).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of PIV data with and without shear.

claim: MDCK cells plated on circular micro-patterns with 500 μm diameter oscillated radially.
source: It has been previously reported that MDCK cells plated on circular micro-patterns with 500 μm diameter, the same as the width of the two planks in our device, oscillated radially, but the origin and mechanism of propagation of these oscillations were unknown (Deforet et al., 2014; Kocgozlu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The origin and mechanism of propagation of oscillations in MDCK cells on circular micro-patterns were unknown.
source: It has been previously reported that MDCK cells plated on circular micro-patterns with 500 μm diameter, the same as the width of the two planks in our device, oscillated radially, but the origin and mechanism of propagation of these oscillations were unknown (Deforet et al., 2014; Kocgozlu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge from prior research.

claim: There were no changes in cell morphology or periodicity that matched long-term y-direction collective oscillations.
source: We found no changes in cell morphology or periodicity that matched long-term y-direction collective oscillations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell segmentation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inward/outward y-direction oscillations within the epithelium primarily represented collective cell movements rather than changes in individual cell morphology.
source: Thus, inward/outward y-direction oscillations within the epithelium primarily represented collective cell movements rather than changes in individual cell morphology.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of morphological changes that correlate with oscillations.

claim: The deformation zone (2–3 cell layers) adjacent to the shear-plane exhibited cell-shape changes and horizontal displacement in the x-direction.
source: While the deformation zone (2–3 cell layers) adjacent to the shear-plane exhibited cell-shape changes and horizontal displacement in the x-direction, this physical shear deformation did not occur (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 5) nor propagate to the rest of the monolayer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell segmentation and imaging data.

claim: Physical shear deformation did not propagate to the rest of the monolayer beyond the deformation zone.
source: While the deformation zone (2–3 cell layers) adjacent to the shear-plane exhibited cell-shape changes and horizontal displacement in the x-direction, this physical shear deformation did not occur (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 5) nor propagate to the rest of the monolayer (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell segmentation analysis showing no morphological changes beyond the deformation zone.

claim: There was no change in the localization of E-cadherin at cell-cell adhesions of migrating cells due to shear.
source: Finally , there was no change in the localization of E-cadherin at cell-cell adhesions of migrating cells due to shear (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The time constant τ is defined as the time to decay by 63% as the epithelium relaxed and remodeled.
source: The measured force peaked (FMAX) immediately after shear, and then relaxed with an exponential decay characteristic of a viscoelastic material, where the time constant, τ, is defined as the time to decay by 63% as the epithelium relaxed and remodeled (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a standard definition for exponential decay time constants.

claim: An additional mechanical element called an inerter, placed in parallel with the viscoelastic components, captured the damped oscillations over tens of hours.
source: Therefore, we inferred that an additional mechanical element was required to capture the time required for mechanical signals to pass through the epithelium, and for the epithelium to generate forces and respond. The addition of a mechanical signal storage and relay element called an inerter, placed in parallel with the viscoelastic components captured these damped oscillations over tens of hours (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mechanical modeling that matches experimental data.

claim: The size of the inerter is inversely proportional to the rate of mechanical signal transduction within the epithelium (80–100 μm/h).
source: The size of the inerter is inversely proportional to the rate of mechanical signal transduction within the epithelium (80–100 μm/h in Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on the relationship between the inerter parameter and observed signal propagation rates.

claim: The addition of an inerter to viscoelastic elements has been suggested before.
source: The addition of an inerter to viscoelastic elements has been suggested before (Popović et al., 2017), but the configuration presented previously did not support the observed oscillations in this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The configuration of inerter with viscoelastic elements presented previously did not support the observed oscillations in this study.
source: The addition of an inerter to viscoelastic elements has been suggested before (Popović et al., 2017), but the configuration presented previously did not support the observed oscillations in this study.
evidence: This claim distinguishes the current model from prior work based on comparison with experimental data.

claim: FINT represents the intrinsic shear force spontaneously generated by an epithelium to maintain an external force balance.
source: In our model, FINT represents the intrinsic shear force spontaneously generated by an epithelium to maintain an external force balance (Prost et al., 2015), and FEXT is the extrinsically applied shear force.
evidence: This claim defines a parameter in the mechanical model based on prior research.

claim: FEXT is the extrinsically applied shear force.
source: In our model, FINT represents the intrinsic shear force spontaneously generated by an epithelium to maintain an external force balance (Prost et al., 2015), and FEXT is the extrinsically applied shear force.
evidence: This claim defines a parameter in the mechanical model.

claim: The FINT required to restore a force balance is 4X smaller than FEXT.
source: Fitting our model with and without FEXT (+Shear, Figure 1D; -Shear, Figure 1H) to observed cell movements, we estimate that the FINT required to restore a force balance is 4X smaller than FEXT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on fitting the mechanical model to experimental data.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in the period or damping rate of oscillations between +Shear and -Shear conditions.
source: There was no statistically significant difference in the period or damping rate of oscillations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, p<0.05), but the amplitude of oscillations was higher with shear than without shear (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The amplitude of oscillations was higher with shear than without shear.
source: There was no statistically significant difference in the period or damping rate of oscillations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, p<0.05), but the amplitude of oscillations was higher with shear than without shear (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The simulation captured the observed long-term oscillations and damping after applied shear.
source: The simulation (Figure 2C,D, Simulation) captured the observed long-term oscillations and damping after applied shear (Figure 2C,D, Experiment).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Addition of blebbistatin before shear inhibited all y-direction oscillatory cell movements, even after washout.
source: Addition of blebbistatin before (Figure 3A,B) or after shear (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) inhibited all y-direction oscillatory cell movements, even after washout.
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data from blebbistatin-treated cells shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Addition of blebbistatin after shear inhibited all y-direction oscillatory cell movements, even after washout.
source: Addition of blebbistatin before (Figure 3A,B) or after shear (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B) inhibited all y-direction oscillatory cell movements, even after washout.
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data from blebbistatin-treated cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: X-direction cell movements in the 2–3 cell layer deformation zone still occurred after treatment with blebbistatin, consistent with deformation of a passive material.
source: Consistent with deformation of a passive material, x-direction cell movements in the 2–3 cell layer deformation zone still occurred after treatment with blebbistatin (Figure 3C,D), although the amount of cell movement was less than in the +Shear condition (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data from blebbistatin-treated cells shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The amount of x-direction cell movement in the deformation zone after blebbistatin treatment was less than in the +Shear condition.
source: Consistent with deformation of a passive material, x-direction cell movements in the 2–3 cell layer deformation zone still occurred after treatment with blebbistatin (Figure 3C,D), although the amount of cell movement was less than in the +Shear condition (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of PIV data between blebbistatin-treated and control conditions.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment revealed no statistical difference in FMAX but a much faster relaxation time (τ = 1.3 min) compared to the +Shear condition (τ = 3.7 min, p<0.01).
source: Sensing data revealed no statistical difference in FMAX but a much faster relaxation time (τ = 1.3 min) compared to the +Shear condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, τ = 3.7 min, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by force sensing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Faster force relaxation time after blebbistatin treatment corresponds to decreased damping in the mechanical model.
source: In our mechanical model, this faster force relaxation time corresponds to decreased damping (c), and the inverse relationship between the size of the inerter and the rate of mechanical signal propagation leads to a much larger inerter value (b) than in the +Shear condition (Figure 3F vs. Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of the mechanical model parameters.

claim: The inverse relationship between the size of the inerter and the rate of mechanical signal propagation leads to a much larger inerter value after blebbistatin treatment than in the +Shear condition.
source: In our mechanical model, this faster force relaxation time corresponds to decreased damping (c), and the inverse relationship between the size of the inerter and the rate of mechanical signal propagation leads to a much larger inerter value (b) than in the +Shear condition (Figure 3F vs. Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of the mechanical model parameters.

claim: Temporary loss of actomyosin contraction, before or after shear, decreases damping, suppresses collective oscillatory behavior, and prevents the propagation of cell movements away from the shear-plane.
source: These results show that temporary loss of actomyosin contraction, before or after shear, decreases damping, suppresses collective oscillatory behavior, and prevents the propagation of cell movements away from the shear-plane.
evidence: This claim summarizes the results from blebbistatin experiments.

claim: E-cadherin in T151 cells has a truncated, nonfunctional extracellular domain, but an intact plasma membrane-tethered cytosolic tail that binds actin through catenins.
source: E-cadherin in T151 cells has a truncated, nonfunctional extracellular domain, but an intact plasma membrane-tethered cytosolic tail that binds actin through catenins (Troxell et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research characterizing T151 cells.

claim: Expression of T151 E-cadherin results in the down-regulation of endogenous E-cadherin, but other cell-cell junctions maintain monolayer cohesion.
source: Importantly, expression of T151 E-cadherin results in the down-regulation of endogenous E-cadherin, but other cell-cell junctions maintain monolayer cohesion (Troxell et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research characterizing T151 cells.

claim: Shear did not induce inward/outward y-direction movements of T151 cells.
source: Shear did not induce inward/outward y-direction movements of T151 cells (Figure 3H,I; Video 6), unlike the +Shear condition in MDCK cells with normal E-cadherin (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data from T151 cells shown in Figure 3H,I.

claim: Extracellular E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion, and not other cell-cell junctions, was specifically required for the propagation of oscillatory y-direction cell movements after shear.
source: This result indicates that extracellular E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion, and not other cell-cell junctions, was specifically required for the propagation of oscillatory y-direction cell movements after shear.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the T151 cell experiments showing lack of oscillations despite intact other junctions.

claim: 2–3 layers of T151 cells adjacent to the shear-plane moved in the x-direction opposite to shear, confirming that passive deformation of the monolayer is independent of E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion.
source: Similar to the blebbistatin-treated epithelium of MDCK cells and the +Shear condition, 2–3 layers of T151 cells adjacent to the shear-plane (<50 μm) moved in the x-direction opposite to shear (Figure 3J,K), confirming that passive deformation of the monolayer is independent of E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data from T151 cells and comparison with other conditions.

claim: T151 cells showed no statistical difference in FMAX and τ compared to the +Shear condition.
source: The sensing data (Figure 3L) revealed no statistical difference in FMAX and τ compared to the +Shear condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by force sensing data and statistical analysis.

claim: Damping is unaffected by the loss of E-cadherin trans-cell binding.
source: Taken together, data from T151 cells demonstrate that damping is unaffected by the loss of E-cadherin trans-cell binding, but E-cadherin transcellular engagement is required to relay the mechanical signal from the shear plane through the epithelium.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the T151 cell experiments showing similar τ values but no oscillations.

claim: E-cadherin transcellular engagement is required to relay the mechanical signal from the shear plane through the epithelium.
source: Taken together, data from T151 cells demonstrate that damping is unaffected by the loss of E-cadherin trans-cell binding, but E-cadherin transcellular engagement is required to relay the mechanical signal from the shear plane through the epithelium.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the T151 cell experiments showing lack of signal propagation.

claim: 200 nM jasplakinolide led to the reorganization of long actin filaments in MDCK cells.
source: We next examined whether shear-induced cell movements were affected by reducing actin dynamics and increasing actin filament length by adding jasplakinolide (200 nM; (Bubb et al., 1994)) 15 min before shear for 1 h (Figure 4A–G; Video 7); immunofluorescence imaging confirmed that 200 nM jasplakinolide led to the reorganization of long actin filaments in this cell type (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: After shear, jasplakinolide treated cells moved inward in the y-direction at a rate (10 μm/h) 3x slower than in the +Shear condition with untreated cells (30 μm/h).
source: After shear, jasplakinolide treated cells moved inward in the y-direction at a rate (10 μm/h; Figure 4A) 3x slower than in the + Shear condition with untreated cells (30 μm/h).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of PIV data from jasplakinolide-treated cells.

claim: Inward movement in jasplakinolide-treated cells propagated to the edge of the plank at a rate 8x faster than the average cell velocity (80 μm/h vs.10 μm/h), but 3.6x slower than the initial rate in the +Shear condition with untreated cells (290 μm/h).
source: This inward movement propagated to the edge of the plank at a rate 8x faster than the average cell velocity (80 μm/h vs.10 μm/h), but 3.6x slower than the initial rate in the + Shear condition with untreated cells (290 μm/h, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of PIV data from jasplakinolide-treated cells.

claim: Jasplakinolide treated cells reversed y-direction movements at 7, 9.5, 13, and 17 hr after shear, but without decreasing velocity magnitude.
source: Jasplakinolide treated cells reversed y-direction movements at 7, 9.5, 13, and 17 hr after shear, but without decreasing velocity magnitude (Figure 4A,B): the magnitude of oscillations was maintained.
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data from jasplakinolide-treated cells shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The magnitude of oscillations was maintained in jasplakinolide-treated cells.
source: Jasplakinolide treated cells reversed y-direction movements at 7, 9.5, 13, and 17 hr after shear, but without decreasing velocity magnitude (Figure 4A,B): the magnitude of oscillations was maintained.
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data from jasplakinolide-treated cells shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: After jasplakinolide treatment, cell movement in the x-direction was opposite to the applied shear, although the x-direction movement propagated to cells further from the shear plane.
source: After jasplakinolide treatment, cell movement in the x-direction was opposite to the applied shear (Figure 4C,D) similar to the +Shear condition with untreated cells (Figure 1F,G), although the x-direction movement propagated to cells further from the shear plane.
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data from jasplakinolide-treated cells shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Regulation of actin dynamics and actin polymer length is involved in propagating and damping shear-induced oscillatory cell movements in both the x- and y-directions.
source: These results indicate that regulation of actin dynamics and actin polymer length is involved in propagating and damping shear-induced oscillatory cell movements in both the x- and y-directions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the jasplakinolide experiments showing altered oscillation dynamics.

claim: Jasplakinolide treatment revealed no statistically significant difference in FMAX, but a much slower relaxation time (τ = 6.2 min) compared to the +Shear condition with untreated cells (τ = 3.7 min).
source: The sensing data from the jasplakinolide treatment revealed no statistically significant difference in FMAX, but a much slower (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, p<0.05) relaxation time (τ = 6.2 min) compared to the +Shear condition with untreated cells (τ = 3.7 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by force sensing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Slower force relaxation time after jasplakinolide treatment corresponds to increased damping in the mechanical model.
source: In our mechanical model, the slower force relaxation time corresponds to an increased damping (c), while the similar rate of mechanical signal propagation (80–100 μm/h) leads to the same inerter value (b) compared to the +Shear condition with untreated cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of the mechanical model parameters.

claim: The similar rate of mechanical signal propagation (80–100 μm/h) after jasplakinolide treatment leads to the same inerter value compared to the +Shear condition with untreated cells.
source: In our mechanical model, the slower force relaxation time corresponds to an increased damping (c), while the similar rate of mechanical signal propagation (80–100 μm/h) leads to the same inerter value (b) compared to the +Shear condition with untreated cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of the mechanical model parameters.

claim: Inward/outward oscillations of jasplakinolide treated cells took much longer to dampen, although with no statistically significant difference in oscillation period compared to the -Shear or +Shear conditions with untreated cells.
source: The vertical average (Figure 4G, Experiment) of y-velocity kymographs (Figure 4A) showed that the inward/outward oscillations of jasplakinolide treated cells took much longer (p<0.05) to dampen, although with no statistically significant difference in oscillation period compared to the -Shear or +Shear conditions with untreated cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Extrapolating from experimental data indicates that oscillations in jasplakinolide-treated cells would have persisted for approximately 80 h after shear.
source: Extrapolating from our experimental data (Figure 4G, Experiment) beyond the period of observation indicates that oscillations would have persisted for approximately 80 h after shear.
evidence: This claim is based on extrapolation of the exponential decay fit to the data.

claim: Jasplakinolide stabilizes and increases actin filament length.
source: Jasplakinolide stabilizes and increases actin filament length (Bubb et al., 1994), which could generate a more viscous actin network that causes the epithelium to act like a material with longer polymeric chains and high damping (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on jasplakinolide's mechanism of action.

claim: Stabilized, longer actin filaments could generate a more viscous actin network that causes the epithelium to act like a material with longer polymeric chains and high damping.
source: Jasplakinolide stabilizes and increases actin filament length (Bubb et al., 1994), which could generate a more viscous actin network that causes the epithelium to act like a material with longer polymeric chains and high damping (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on polymer physics.

claim: Normal actin filament dynamics and turnover may be required for oscillation damping and dissipation of the mechanical signal generated by shear, which are required to reach a new force balance.
source: Thus, normal actin filament dynamics and turnover may be required for oscillation damping and dissipation of the mechanical signal generated by shear, which are required to reach a new force balance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the jasplakinolide experiments showing prolonged oscillations.

claim: Changes in cell density over the time of the experiment did not affect the response of the epithelium to shear.
source: We can rule out the possibility that changes in cell density over the time of the experiment affected the response of the epithelium to shear.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of cell density data across conditions.

claim: Little or no cell extrusion of dead cells was detected.
source: We detected little or no cell extrusion of dead cells (Video 1), and the amount of cell division was similar under all experimental conditions with or without shear (Videos 1 and 3–7).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual evidence from videos.

claim: The amount of cell division was similar under all experimental conditions with or without shear.
source: We detected little or no cell extrusion of dead cells (Video 1), and the amount of cell division was similar under all experimental conditions with or without shear (Videos 1 and 3–7).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual evidence from videos.

claim: The cell density was between 6,000–10,000 cells/mm2, due to temporary local variations, regardless of the application of shear.
source: Furthermore, the cell density was between 6,000–10,000 cells/mm2, due to temporary local variations, regardless of the application of shear (Figure 1—figure supplement 4vs. Figure 1—figure supplement 6), and either in the presence of blebbistatin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) or jasplakinolide (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell density measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Local shear affects the epithelium in two spatially and temporally distinct phases, each with different dependencies on the actin cytoskeleton and E-cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion.
source: Collectively, our results support the idea that local shear affects the epithelium in two spatially and temporally distinct phases, each with different dependencies on the actin cytoskeleton and E-cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion.
evidence: This claim summarizes the overall findings from all experimental conditions.

claim: X-direction movements and deformations in 2–3 cell layers adjacent to the shear-plane are independent of the organization and contraction of the actin cytoskeleton, and E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion.
source: In one phase, x-direction movements and deformations in 2–3 cell layers adjacent to the shear-plane are independent of the organization and contraction of the actin cytoskeleton, and E-cadherin trans-cell adhesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations that x-direction movements occurred in blebbistatin-treated and T151 cells.

claim: X-direction movements in the deformation zone last several minutes, and do not oscillate except when actin dynamics are disrupted.
source: These movements last several minutes, and do not oscillate except when actin dynamics are disrupted.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of x-direction movements over time in different conditions.

claim: Y-direction cell movements in the epithelium behave as a damped oscillator, requiring actomyosin contraction, actin filament dynamics, and E-cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion.
source: In another phase, y-direction cell movements in the epithelium behave as a damped oscillator, requiring actomyosin contraction, actin filament dynamics, and E-cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion; these movements persist for tens of hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with blebbistatin, jasplakinolide, and T151 cells.

claim: Y-direction cell movements persist for tens of hours.
source: In another phase, y-direction cell movements in the epithelium behave as a damped oscillator, requiring actomyosin contraction, actin filament dynamics, and E-cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion; these movements persist for tens of hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by long-term imaging data showing oscillations over 20+ hours.

claim: Transient local deformation of 2–3 cell layers adjacent to the shear-plane generates a mechanical event that is relayed across the epithelium over tens of hours.
source: Based upon our simulations and experimental data, we suggest that transient local deformation of 2–3 cell layers adjacent to the shear-plane generates a mechanical event that is relayed across the epithelium over tens of hours.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on integration of experimental and modeling results.

claim: Cell movements at the shear-plane may induce tension on E-cadherin in cells adjacent to the deformation zone.
source: Cell movements at the shear-plane may induce tension on E-cadherin in cells adjacent to the deformation zone, and tension on E-cadherin increases actomyosin contraction and cell stiffening (Borghi et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2014; le Duc et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on prior research on E-cadherin mechanotransduction.

claim: Tension on E-cadherin increases actomyosin contraction and cell stiffening.
source: Cell movements at the shear-plane may induce tension on E-cadherin in cells adjacent to the deformation zone, and tension on E-cadherin increases actomyosin contraction and cell stiffening (Borghi et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2014; le Duc et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mechanical event from the deformed cells is transmitted throughout the epithelium via direct coupling of actomyosin contraction and E-cadherin cell-cell adhesion.
source: Therefore, we suggest that the mechanical event from the deformed cells is transmitted throughout the epithelium via direct coupling of actomyosin contraction and E-cadherin cell-cell adhesion (Borghi et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2014; le Duc et al., 2010; Yonemura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on integration of experimental results and prior research.

claim: A temporary (1 h) loss of actomyosin contraction blocked long-term (24 h) y-direction cell oscillations even though actomyosin contraction was re-established after blebbistatin washout.
source: Note that a temporary (1 h) loss of actomyosin contraction blocked long-term (24 h) y-direction cell oscillations even though actomyosin contraction was re-established after blebbistatin washout (+Blebb; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from blebbistatin washout experiments.

claim: With the loss of actomyosin contractility, the generated mechanical signal dissipated, which enabled the epithelium to immediately reach a new external force balance.
source: These data indicate that with the loss of actomyosin contractility, the generated mechanical signal dissipated, which enabled the epithelium to immediately reach a new external force balance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the blebbistatin experiments showing no oscillations after washout.

claim: Dissipation of the mechanical signal under the -Shear and +Shear conditions occurred through oscillatory cell movements over >15 h, which gradually damped global cell movements as a new external force balance was reached.
source: We suggest that dissipation of the mechanical signal under the -Shear and +Shear conditions occurred through oscillatory cell movements over >15 h, which gradually damped global cell movements as a new external force balance was reached.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on the observed damped oscillations.

claim: The longer force relaxation time constant for cells treated with jasplakinolide showed that damping was significantly increased.
source: The longer force relaxation time constant for cells treated with jasplakinolide showed that damping was significantly increased (Figure 4E) because of the longer, stable actin filaments that formed in the presence of jaspakinolide (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by force sensing data and immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: The novel device and results answer the question of how local shear on cells induces global changes in multicellular organization.
source: In summary, our novel device and results answer the question of how local shear on cells induces global changes in multicellular organization.
evidence: This claim summarizes the overall contribution of the study.

claim: A force imbalance is generated through local deformation of a few cells by shear.
source: Mechanistically, a force imbalance is generated through local deformation of a few cells by shear.
evidence: This claim is a mechanistic summary based on experimental observations.

claim: The sensing and restoration of force imbalance requires tension developed by actomyosin contraction linked to E-cadherin cell-cell adhesion.
source: The sensing and restoration of this force imbalance requires tension developed by actomyosin contraction linked to E-cadherin cell-cell adhesion.
evidence: This claim is a mechanistic summary based on experiments with blebbistatin and T151 cells.

claim: The results provide new insights into the mechanical basis of collective cell movement in tissues.
source: Our results provide new insights into the mechanical basis of collective cell movement in tissues.
evidence: This claim summarizes the overall significance of the study.

claim: MDCK type GII cells stably expressing E-cadherin:DsRed were cultured at 37°C and 5% CO2 in DMEM low-glucose medium supplemented with 10% FBS, 250 μg/mL G418, and antibiotics.
source: Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) type GII cells stably expressing E-cadherin:DsRed (Troxell et al., 2000) or truncated E-cadherin (T151, under control of a doxycycline-repressible promoter, Troxell et al., 2000) were cultured at 37°C and 5% CO2 in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) low-glucose (200 mg/L) medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (MDCK Ecad:DsRed) or tetracycline-free FBS (Clonetech, 631106) (T151), 250 μg/mL G418, and 1 g/L sodium bicarbonate, penicillin (30 μg/mL), kanamycin (1 mg/mL), and streptomycin (30 μg/mL).
evidence: This claim describes the cell culture methods used in the study.

claim: Silicon Microelectromechanical Systems devices were fabricated at the Stanford Nanofabrication Facility from 4-inch silicon wafers (50 μm device layer).
source: Silicon Microelectromechanical Systems devices were fabricated at the Stanford Nanofabrication Facility from 4-inch silicon wafers (50 μm device layer) using principles and methods presented previously (Mukundan and Pruitt, 2009; Sadeghipour et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim describes the device fabrication methods.

claim: Devices were coated with collagen (50 μg/mL in 0.01% acetic acid for 1 hr at room temperature).
source: Newly fabricated devices were hydrated in 70% ethanol, rinsed in MilliQ water, and rinsed in 0.01% acetic acid prior to coating with collagen (Corning, 354236, 50 μg/mL in 0.01% acetic acid for 1 hr at room temperature).
evidence: This claim describes the device preparation methods.

claim: Cells were seeded at a concentration of 1.5 × 10^6 cells/mL in low-calcium (5 μM Ca++) DMEM.
source: Cell monolayers were dissociated with 0.05% trypsin-EDTA (Life Technologies, 25300–062) for 6 min at 37°C. Cells were resuspended at a concentration of 1.5 × 106 cells/mL in low-calcium (5 μM Ca++) DMEM.
evidence: This claim describes the cell seeding methods.

claim: Approximately 2700 cells were pipetted onto the two combined 1000 × 250 μm planks of the device.
source: A glass capillary tube with an inner diameter of 500 μm was attached to a Rainin p10 micropipette tip. Using a turn-dial micropipette,~2700 cells were pipetted onto the two combined 1000 × 250 μm planks of the device, which was submerged in DMEM imaging medium plus 1.8 mM Ca++.
evidence: This claim describes the cell seeding methods.

claim: Shear was applied after 18 hr of cell adhesion.
source: After 1 hr, the medium was agitated to remove non-adherent cells; shear was applied after a further 18 hr.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental timeline.

claim: The rate of shear displacement was ~20 μm/s.
source: The actuating plank was displaced 100 μm in the positive x-direction and held for the duration of the experiment (24 hr), which caused in-plane shear deformation at the mid-plane of the monolayer. The rate of shear displacement was ~20 μm/s.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method for applying shear.

claim: The 100 μm in-plane shear did not rupture individual cells, cell-cell adhesions, or the cell monolayer as a whole.
source: The 100 μm in-plane shear did not rupture individual cells, cell-cell adhesions, or the cell monolayer as a whole.
evidence: This claim is supported by visual observations during experiments.

claim: Cells were imaged with a Leica DM-RXA2 microscope and a Hamamatsu Orca-R2 camera at 37°C.
source: Cells were imaged with a Leica DM-RXA2 microscope and a Hamamatsu Orca-R2 camera encased in a black acrylic incubator at 37°C achieved using an Air-Therm ATX.
evidence: This claim describes the imaging methods.

claim: A Leica fluorescent 10x objective was used for all experiments.
source: A Leica fluorescent 10x objective was used for all experiments.
evidence: This claim describes the imaging methods.

claim: Images were taken for 45 min at 5 min intervals, and for 15 min at 30 s intervals for a total of 1 hr prior to the application of shear.
source: Images were taken for 45 min at 5 min intervals, and for 15 min at 30 s intervals for a total of 1 hr prior to the application of shear.
evidence: This claim describes the imaging timeline.

claim: Images during shear were captured at 200 ms intervals and binned by 2 × 2 for a final resolution of 2.12 pixels/μm.
source: Images during shear were captured at 200 ms intervals and binned by 2 × 2 for a final resolution of 2.12 pixels/μm.
evidence: This claim describes the imaging methods during shear application.

claim: Immediately after shear, images were captured every 30 s for 45 min, and then every 5 min for 23.25 hr.
source: Immediately after shear, images were captured every 30 s for 45 min, and then every 5 min for 23.25 hr.
evidence: This claim describes the imaging timeline after shear.

claim: Fluorescent cell boundaries of MDCK E-cadherin:DsRed cells were used to segment individual cells in the monolayer using custom MATLAB code.
source: Fluorescent cell boundaries of MDCK E-cadherin:DsRed cells were used to segment individual cells in the monolayer using custom MATLAB code (Sadeghipour and Garcia, 2018) based on techniques presented previously (Harris et al., 2012; Hart et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim describes the cell segmentation methods.

claim: PIV was performed using MATLAB PIVlab 1.41.
source: PIV was performed using MATLAB PIVlab 1.41 (The MathWorks).
evidence: This claim describes the PIV analysis methods.

claim: An FFT window deformation PIV algorithm was used with a first pass interrogation size of 120 pixels with step size 60 pixels, and a second pass interrogation of 48 pixels with a step size of 24 pixels.
source: An Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) window deformation PIV algorithm was used with a first pass interrogation size of 120 pixels with step size 60 pixels, and a second pass interrogation of 48 pixels with a step size of 24 pixels.
evidence: This claim describes the PIV analysis parameters.

claim: For the mechanical model, stiffness (k) was held constant across experimental conditions.
source: For the mechanical model, stiffness (k) was held constant across experimental conditions, and damping (c) was calculated based on c = kD, from the equation for an exponentially damped sinusoidal function (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim describes the mechanical modeling approach.

claim: Damping (c) was calculated based on c = kD, from the equation for an exponentially damped sinusoidal function.
source: For the mechanical model, stiffness (k) was held constant across experimental conditions, and damping (c) was calculated based on c = kD, from the equation for an exponentially damped sinusoidal function (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim describes the mechanical modeling approach.

claim: The value of the inerter (b) was inversely related to the rate of propagation within the epithelium.
source: The value of the inerter (b) was inversely related to the rate of propagation within the epithelium, which led to an effectively infinite value where the rate of propagation was zero (+Blebb, Figure 3A; T151, Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim describes the mechanical modeling approach.

claim: When the rate of propagation was not zero, the value of the inerter (b) was chosen to achieve a mechanical system with an intrinsic period (P) of 8 hr, where b = kP2/(4π2).
source: When the rate of propagation was not zero (+Shear, Figure 1D; -Shear, 1H; and +Jasp, Figure 4A), the value of the inerter (b) was chosen to achieve a mechanical system with an intrinsic period (P) of 8 hr, where b = kP2/(4π2), based on the statistical tests performed and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This claim describes the mechanical modeling approach.

claim: Statistical significance of the results was analyzed using a combination of the Kruskal-Wallis and the Mann-Whitney U tests.
source: Statistical significance of the results was analyzed using a combination of the Kruskal-Wallis and the Mann-Whitney U tests.
evidence: This claim describes the statistical analysis methods.

claim: Non-parametric statistical tests are appropriate when data are not normally distributed.
source: These non-parametric statistical tests are appropriate when data are not normally distributed.
evidence: This claim is based on established statistical principles.
